That is the cost of patience, and I accept it, because the alternative is paying up for a spent catalyst three days before a quarter management has already told me will be soft.

One last thing for the director, on the question that actually decides whether this is cheap or a trap. The obvious fear is the energy transition, and it is why the multiple is 8.7 rather than 15. I judge that threat manageable rather than terminal, and the reasoning matters more than the label: the asset is the store, not the pump — 7-Eleven is remodelling 7,000 sites through 2030 for reasons unrelated to what fills the tank; the payment terminal, the site software and the car-wash brain get paid regardless of energy type; Driivz is the number-two charging-management platform globally at ~110,000 plugs and won Iberdrola/bp pulse's 2,500 fast chargers on 1 July 2026; and underground tanks must be monitored while they exist, which will be decades. The honest bear case here is not 'this melts.' It is 'this never grows, and you are paid 10% a year in cash to wait for a re-rating nobody can force.' That is a price objection, not a quality objection — which is why the value score is a 4 and the moat cap does not bite. But it is also exactly why this is a 3 on the whole and a wait-for-the-flush rather than a buy-now: a company whose value must be harvested by buyback arithmetic over years, rather than released by an event over months, should be bought on a bad day, and 30 July is the most likely bad day on the calendar.
sop_fair_value: $41 a share (about 34% above the $30.60 price on 16 July 2026)
sop_breakdown:
The parts, valued on enterprise-value-to-EBITDA and then netted for debt. Environmental and Fueling Solutions — Gilbarco dispensers plus Veeder-Root tank gauges — is the crown jewel and about two-thirds of the value: ~$505M of estimated 2026 EBITDA at 11x = ~$5.56B, justified by a ~30% margin, majority share, and a regulation-driven 350,000-unit upgrade cycle management calls early innings. Mobility Technologies — Invenco payments, DRB car wash, Driivz charging software — contributes ~$230M at 10.5x = ~$2.42B; it grew 22% organically in 2025 with 35% recurring revenue and a contractual attach to every U.S. dispenser, which merits the software-adjacent multiple, but its order flow is lumpy and Driivz remains unquantified. Repair Solutions (Matco Tools) contributes ~$125M at 6x = ~$0.75B — a deliberately low multiple for a franchised tool distributor with a wage-pressured customer, soft sell-out and a brand-new outside president. Unallocated corporate cost of ~−$105M capitalized at 10x subtracts ~$1.05B. That sums to an enterprise value of ~$7.68B. Subtract $1.70B of net debt (borrowings $1.90B plus $38M of capitalized leases, less $234M of cash, as of 3 April 2026 — the inclusive definition; filings often quote the ~$1.67B figure excluding leases) to reach ~$5.98B of equity, or ~$42.5 across ~141M shares. Add ~$1.0 a share for the Teletrac consideration still held as paper — the $100M seller's note plus the retained ~30% stake, marked conservatively — to reach ~$43.5.

I then trim to $41 and use that as the base case. The trim is deliberate and I want to be explicit about it rather than hide it in a multiple: this spin-legacy discount has not closed in the six years since Fortive separated the company in 2020, the terminal-value discount for a fuel-dispenser installed base is partly legitimate rather than wholly irrational, and 2.2 times net leverage is heavier than the peer set carries. A fair value the stock has never sustainably traded at deserves a haircut, not a footnote.

That $41 lands close to the street's $41.20 consensus, but it arrives from a different direction and I am not deferring to it: the street's median is $37 and its newest print is KeyBanc's $35.00 on 13 July 2026. I am above the marginal analyst, below the year-ago average of $44.33.

Sanity-checks against the peer set: $41 is 11.7 times 2026 adjusted earnings of ~$3.50, 8.9 times free cash flow of ~$460M, and 9.9 times EBITDA at the enterprise level. Dover, Fortive and ITT trade around 18-22 times free cash flow and roughly 14-17 times EBITDA; IDEX and Roper are higher still. In other words the base case does not require Vontier to close the peer gap — it requires the gap to narrow from roughly half the peer multiple to roughly two-thirds of it.
risk_reward: Downside to the adverse case is $30.60 to $23.00, a fall of about 25%, and there is no structural floor beneath it — no net cash, no deal terms, no tender; net debt of $1.70B means the debt comes off the top, and the $1.0B buyback authorization is discretionary policy, not a contractual backstop. Upside to the $41 base case is about 34% over roughly 18 months, with the $52 favourable case requiring a genuine convergence toward peer multiples. While waiting, the holder is paid roughly an 11% free-cash-flow yield, most of which management has demonstrated it will spend retiring stock. The honest characterisation is a modestly favourable but not compelling skew on a slow fuse: the asymmetry is real but it is arithmetic, not event-driven, and nothing on the calendar forces it to resolve.
peer_comps_note:
The peer file supplies no live override multiples and no anchor multiple, so I built the sum-of-the-parts from segment multiples of my own and used the peer set only as a sanity-check rather than as the anchor — the right order of operations given that peer multiples de-rate and a stale anchor would inflate the apparent discount.

The peer verdict is 'cheap versus peers,' and the direction holds: Vontier's 9.9 times price-to-free-cash-flow is roughly half the ~18-22 times of Dover, Fortive and ITT, and a third of IDEX and Roper at ~28-30 times, against a respectable 47.2% gross margin and 12.8% return on invested capital. But the peer file's own caveat is the honest part and I want to sharpen it. Two-thirds of the gap is earned, not mispriced, and a director should not treat the full spread as alpha:

First, growth. Dover, Fortive, IDEX and Roper are compounders. Vontier's revenue is $3.08B against $2.99B four years ago — a −1.2% three-year compound rate. Half of a compounder's multiple is arithmetically defensible for a company that does not compound revenue.

Second, quality of returns. Roper earns 25%-plus on invested capital; Vontier earns 12.8%. The 51.4% return on equity is a buyback artifact from a shrunk equity base, not an earnings-power signal, and comparing it to peer returns on equity would be an error.

Third, mix. Roughly a fifth of Vontier is Matco Tools, a franchised hand-tool distributor with a wage-pressured customer — a business none of these peers owns and none of these multiples contemplate.

Fourth, leverage. Net debt of $1.70B is roughly 2.2 times EBITDA, heavier than the peer set.

This is not the shared-factor problem — Vontier's discount is idiosyncratic, not sector beta. Dover, Fortive, IDEX and ITT are not de-rated; they trade at full multiples today. The gap is single-name, which means it is genuinely available if it closes. My base case does not require it to close: at $41 Vontier would trade at ~8.9 times free cash flow against the peer set's 18-22 times, moving from roughly half the peer multiple to roughly two-thirds. That is the discount narrowing from unjustified to merely justified — a much lower bar than convergence, and the reason I am comfortable at a $41 base rather than the $43.5 the raw parts produce.

One live market test deserves more weight than any peer multiple: Teletrac Navman, a fixed and cash-generative asset, sold on 6 July 2026 for $220M of headline value but only $80M of cash, with $140M in a seller's note and retained equity. In the hottest merger market on record, that is the only recent independent appraisal of a Vontier asset, and it argues the private market does not pay peer multiples for these parts either.

bull_thesis:
The bull case is that the market is pricing Vontier as a melting fuel-pump maker when what it actually owns is a regulated, contractually-attached convenience-store infrastructure annuity that throws off cash and is buying back its own stock at a tenth of earnings.

Start with the price. At $30.60 a share on the New York Stock Exchange (16 July 2026 close), Vontier's roughly 141 million shares are worth about $4.31B. Management guided to double-digit adjusted earnings growth in 2026 off the $3.20 a share it delivered in 2025 (the four quarters printed $0.77, $0.79, $0.78 and $0.86) — call it about $3.50. That is 8.7 times forward earnings. On cash it is starker: adjusted free cash flow (the cash left after running and investing in the business) was over $460M in 2025, about 15% of sales, and grew 27.9% year over year with a three-year compound rate of 19.1%. Against a $4.31B market value that is a free-cash-flow yield near 11%. Diversified industrial-technology peers — Dover, Fortive (Vontier's former parent), ITT — trade around 18-22 times free cash flow; IDEX and Roper are 28-30 times and up.

Why the base is not melting. Three pieces of evidence from the calls, in ascending order of importance:

First, the demand driver is store capital spending, not fuel volume. Convenience retail is about two-thirds of sales and is growing at a mid-single-digit rate on food service and technology. 7-Eleven has publicly committed to remodel 7,000 North American stores through 2030 plus 1,300 new sites (cited by management, Q1 2026). That capital budget does not care what fills the tank. Management put dated numbers behind the resilience claim on the first-quarter 2026 call: this end market has been durable through 25 years of volatility, and high oil prices have historically been a net positive because fatter fuel margins fund store investment. Environmental and Fueling Solutions has grown at roughly a 6% organic compound rate over the last two years and delivered low-double-digit dispenser growth globally in the first quarter of 2026 with segment margin flat at nearly 30%.

Second, the compliance revenue is regulated. Veeder-Root's automated tank gauges are the instrument that monitors underground fuel storage, with an installed base of over 350,000 units globally, a CARB certification requirement, and a replacement cycle management describes as early innings and 'a pretty steady replacement cycle over the next five plus years' (Q3 2025). One of the largest North American convenience operators signed up to upgrade its entire base across 4,500 sites over five years (Q2 2025). Underground tanks must be monitored while they exist, and they will exist for decades.

Third — and this is the load-bearing fact of the whole thesis — the payments attach is contractual. Asked directly in the fourth quarter of 2025 whether the terminals were a low-margin giveaway used to buy recurring revenue, the chief financial officer answered: 'we sell dispensers with payments. There is no option in the U.S. to buy a dispenser without our payments.' Every dispenser Vontier ships in its majority-share home market pulls an Invenco payment kit with it. Invenco closed 2025 at nearly $650M of revenue, up 22% organically, with recurring revenue at about 35% of its base growing 17%, having passed a billion transactions on its payment servers. Over 50% of new dispensers now leave the factory with a FlexPay 6 unit. The customer's own switching cost is the payment certification bill — 'hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars annually' — which Vontier's single-architecture platform collapses. That is a genuine switching-cost moat, and it is getting deeper as the platform extends to in-store terminals (launched Q4 2025), car washes and chargers.

Why earnings grow even if revenue does not. Vontier's algorithm is margin plus share count, and both are live. Management committed to 80 basis points of operating margin expansion at the midpoint in 2026 and $15M of in-year savings, phased publicly ($1M in Q1, about $3M in Q2, the balance in the back half). It has kept this kind of promise before: roughly $50M of tariff cost was quantified in the first quarter of 2025, mitigated through supply-chain moves and price, and the gross margin held at 47.2% while China procurement was cut to under $50M on a run-rate basis. On capital, the board raised the repurchase authorization to $1.0B on 19 May 2026 — about 23% of the entire market value — and this management actually spends it (roughly $175M through the third quarter of 2025). Book value per share has compounded at 26% over five years. At $30 a share, every dollar of that authorization retires more stock than it did at $45.

The portfolio is being cleaned. The European service business, two non-core assets and a minority equity stake went in 2025; Teletrac Navman — announced 7 May 2026 at a $220M valuation — completed on 6 July 2026, bringing $80M of cash, a $100M seller's note and a retained ~30% stake. Management said the cash goes to 'additional share repurchases and selective bolt-on acquisitions.'

The electric-vehicle question is hedged, not ignored. Driivz manages roughly 110,000 charging plugs and is the number-two platform globally, winning dated business through 2026 (Iberdrola/bp pulse's 2,500 fast chargers on 1 July 2026; Duracell E-Charge's UK network on 11 May 2026). If the forecourt electrifies, Vontier still sells the payment terminal, the site software and the car wash brain.

Conditions that must hold: convenience-retail capital spending stays constructive through 2027; the back-half-weighted $15M savings actually lands and the first-quarter margin miss proves to be mix and research-spend timing as claimed; Invenco's order lumpiness does not turn into order loss; and the board keeps buying stock aggressively at these levels rather than spending the authorization on acquisitions.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is simple and it has been right for four years: Vontier does not grow, cannot force anyone to notice, and the discount is not a mistake — it is the market's price for a flat business with a finite runway and no clock on it.

Start with the number management does not lead with. Revenue was $2.99B in 2021 and $3.08B in 2025. That is +0.7% in total across four years — a three-year revenue compound rate of −1.2%. Across five consecutive earnings calls management has promised 'sustainable above-market growth.' The market is not disputing the adjective; it is disputing the noun. Reported earnings per share went from $2.43 in 2021 to $2.76 in 2025, a 3.5% compound rate. The 11% adjusted growth management celebrates is margin and buyback arithmetic performed on a stationary base. Buy this and you are underwriting a financial engine, not a business engine — and financial engines re-rate only when someone forces them to.

Nobody is going to force it. This is the heart of the bear case. The one hard, dated corporate event in the file has already happened: the Teletrac divestiture closed on 6 July 2026, and the stock is $30.60 — near its 52-week low of $27.25, 18% below its 200-day average, and sitting 12% up its 52-week range. The re-rate did not come. What remains is a $1.0B repurchase authorization, which is a policy, not a promise: no contractual obligation, no deadline, no minimum. Management has been telling anyone who will listen that the stock is too cheap — 'our shares remain meaningfully discounted to peers, underscoring the upside as we continue to execute' (Q3 2025 closing remarks) — which is exactly what a management team says when it has run out of levers. It has been saying it for three quarters and the stock has gone down.

And the people who would know are not buying. Zero open-market insider purchases against three sales totalling 24,097 shares. The chief executive calls his own stock meaningfully discounted and buys none of it.

The Teletrac terms tell you what the assets are actually worth. In the hottest merger market on record — roughly $2.8T announced in the first half of 2026 — a business management describes as a completed multi-year turnaround with reduced churn, mid-single-digit recurring-revenue growth and positive free cash flow fetched $220M of headline value but only $80M of cash. The other $140M is a seller's note plus a retained 30% stake. That is what a seller accepts when the cash bid is not there. It is a live, dated data point that the sum-of-the-parts is worth less than the parts-multiple exercise implies — and it is the only recent market test of any Vontier asset.

The operating story is already cracking. In the first quarter of 2026, adjusted operating margin declined 70 basis points 'below our expectations' — the first internal miss in the file, and it was disclosed on the same morning as the divestiture announcement, which is how you bury a miss. Adjusted earnings of $0.80 missed the $0.82 the street wanted. Meanwhile the Investor Day promise of 150 basis points of margin expansion over three years, reaffirmed as recently as the second quarter of 2025, has been silently replaced by 80 basis points for 2026 and $15M of savings — a target cut roughly in half with no reconciliation, and no analyst has made them bridge it. Cash conversion was walked down twice in one quarter: 100% to 95% to 'greater than 90% through 2028.'

The next quarter is guided down. Management told the street on 7 May 2026 to expect core sales down about 1% in the second quarter, with Mobility Technologies down low-to-mid single digits against a $25M Vehicle Identification Solution shipment comparison, and about $11M of the $15M savings programme still unproven in the back half. Vontier reports on 30 July 2026 against a $0.82 consensus. A second consecutive margin miss is a live possibility, and the analyst community is already backing away: twelve price targets over the past year averaged $44.33; the last two average $39.00; KeyBanc cut to $35.00 on 13 July 2026 with the stock at $29.42. Target velocity is −14%. The sell side is walking its numbers down toward the price, not up toward the thesis.

A fifth of the company is genuinely impaired. Matco Tools sells hand tools off franchisee trucks to wage-pressured auto technicians. Sell-out was down about 5% in the first half of 2025; management called the consumer 'a harder time with their pocketbook' and admitted in the fourth quarter of 2025, 'I do not really know what is going on with the consumer this year.' An outside transformation specialist was hired to run it on 22 June 2026. That is either a fix or a preparation for a sale — and if the sale is priced like Teletrac's, it will not be a windfall.

The terminal question is real, and being cheap does not answer it. The installed base is fuel dispensers and underground petroleum tanks. Over a fifteen-to-twenty-year horizon, electrification shrinks the fuelling stops, the fuel volume and eventually the tank count. The hedge — Driivz — is unquantified: management gave it a full, enthusiastic answer in the first quarter of 2025 ('#2 worldwide... it is a SaaS business at very high margins... it will actually begin to show up at the Vontier level') and has not put a revenue number on it in a single call since, while continuing to issue press releases about it. Driivz's own 2026 industry report concedes the charging market is shifting 'from rapid infrastructure build-out toward intelligent profitability' — which is a polite way of saying the build-out is slowing. A company that stopped quantifying its growth engine on the calls but keeps marketing it in press releases is telling you something.

The balance sheet removes the margin for error. Net debt is $1.70B (borrowings of $1.90B plus $38M of capitalized leases, less $234M of cash) — roughly 2.2 times earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, against peers who carry less. Semi-annual bond interest is about $19M a payment. Altman-Z of 2.8 is the grey zone, not the safe zone. There is no net cash cushion; in a sum-of-the-parts, the debt comes off the top.

What would confirm the bear: a second margin miss on 30 July; core sales worse than the guided −1%; the $15M savings slipping out of 2026; the buyback pace lagging its $1.0B authorization while cash goes into bolt-on acquisitions instead; or a Matco divestiture at a Teletrac-style paper-heavy price.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market: the street is pricing Vontier's terminal decade into its next twelve months, and it is pricing the wrong asset.

The explicit street position is visible and it is drifting the wrong way. Twelve price targets over the past year averaged $44.33; the last five average $38.20; the last two average $39.00; and the newest — KeyBanc, 13 July 2026 — cut to $35.00 with the stock at $29.42. Target velocity is −14%. The median target is $37 against a $41.20 consensus, which means the average is being held up by a stale high ($55) and one fresh outlier (Nigel Coe's $43.00 on 9 July 2026). The marginal analyst is capitulating toward the price. Consensus forward earnings growth is +8.9% against management's double-digit guide — the street does not believe the guide either.

Three specific assumptions embedded in that positioning are, on the evidence, factually wrong:

First, the market treats Vontier as levered to fuel volume. It is levered to convenience-store capital budgets, which are a different and currently accelerating variable. Roughly two-thirds of sales sit in an end market growing at a mid-single-digit rate on food service and technology investment, with 7-Eleven alone publicly committed to remodelling 7,000 North American stores through 2030 plus 1,300 new builds. Environmental and Fueling has compounded at roughly 6% organically over two years and grew dispensers at a low-double-digit rate globally in the first quarter of 2026. The pump is the smallest reason a convenience chain writes a cheque to Vontier.

Second, and most valuable: the market reads higher oil as a Vontier headwind. Management's inverted argument — laid out in full on the first-quarter 2026 call, and consistent with 25 years of end-market history — is that higher retail fuel prices produce fatter operator margins, more frequent visits and a trade-down effect into convenience stores, all of which fund the modernisation capital spending that Vontier sells into. Management also noted that operators plan capital 'two or three years in advance... oil price volatility does not really change their longer-term CapEx plans.' In a regime where oil is the shared macro factor everyone is watching, owning an asset whose driver runs opposite to the naive read is worth something on its own.

Third, the market prices the payments business as a hardware accessory. It is a contractual attach: 'we sell dispensers with payments. There is no option in the U.S. to buy a dispenser without our payments' (Q4 2025). Invenco is a nearly $650M business that grew 22% organically in 2025 with 35% recurring revenue growing 17%, and its customers' switching cost is a payment-certification bill running 'hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars annually.' Embedded inside an 8.7-times-earnings industrial, that is not being valued at all.

But here is where I part company with the bulls, and it is the reason this is not a top-conviction call. The street is not wrong about the thing that actually matters most: Vontier does not grow its revenue, and it has not for four years. $2.99B in 2021, $3.08B in 2025. Management has said 'above-market growth' on five consecutive calls while the top line stood still. Half of the discount to Dover, Fortive and ITT is arithmetically earned by that fact, and another slice is earned by 12.8% returns on invested capital versus Roper's 25%-plus, by a fifth of the company being a franchised tool distributor, and by 2.2 times net leverage. The mispricing is the difference between the discount being justified and the discount being roughly double what it should be. That is a real gap, worth about a third of the price, and it is not the same thing as a hidden compounder.
forcing_function:
There isn't one with teeth, and no amount of good analysis manufactures one. This is the crux of the call.

The hard, dated event has already fired. Teletrac Navman closed on 6 July 2026 — announced 7 May at $220M, delivered roughly a week past the guided June close. The stock did not move; it sits at $30.60, near its 52-week low. When a company executes its catalyst on schedule and the stock stays at the low, the market is telling you it was not the catalyst.

What is actually on the calendar, in descending order of force:

**30 July 2026 — second-quarter results.** Hard and dated, consensus $0.82. But this is a disclosure, not a catalyst, and management has pre-guided it down (core sales about −1%, Mobility Technologies down low-to-mid single digits on the $25M comparison). Its function in this thesis is inverted: it is more likely to produce the entry price than the re-rating. The specific thing to watch is whether the 70-basis-point first-quarter margin miss repeats. If margin recovers as management claims — mix and research-spend timing — the 2026 guide of 80 basis points of expansion and double-digit earnings growth is intact and the 8.7-times multiple starts to look indefensible. If it misses twice, the stock breaks $27.25 and the wait was correct.

**The $1.0B buyback — the real lever, on no clock.** Approved 19 May 2026, roughly 23% of the market value. This is the mechanism by which the value gets realised whether or not the multiple ever re-rates: flat revenue plus expanding margin plus a shrinking share count is 8-11% earnings growth a year, and at $30 the authorization retires more stock than the board budgeted for. But it is discretionary policy — no obligation, no deadline, no minimum — and management may divert it to bolt-on acquisitions, which it has explicitly reserved the right to do. A powerful engine with no ignition date.

**Further portfolio actions — unannounced and speculative.** Matco Tools is the obvious next candidate: management hired an outside transformation specialist, Cameron Richardson, as its Group President on 22 June 2026, which is what you do either to fix a business or to dress it for sale. Removing a fifth of revenue that is consumer-cyclical, low-multiple and off-strategy would leave a cleaner convenience-retail infrastructure company that is far easier for the market to multiple correctly. But nothing has been announced, and the Teletrac terms — only $80M of the $220M in cash, the rest in a seller's note and retained equity, struck in the hottest merger market on record — are a live warning about what these parts actually fetch.

**Activism is the missing party, and its absence is data.** By Loeb's Third Point criteria this should be a target: a demonstrable sum-of-the-parts discount, a chief executive publicly complaining about his own multiple ('our shares remain meaningfully discounted to peers,' Q3 2025), a low-multiple orphan segment, and a regime in which activism is running at 136 global campaigns in the first half of 2026 with 'sell yourself' the single most common demand at 21%. Yet no campaign has surfaced. Either the activists have looked and concluded the parts do not fetch more than the whole — which the Teletrac terms support — or the $4.31B market value is too small to interest the funds that could force it. Neither reading is bullish, and I will not model an activist that has not appeared.

**What I am explicitly not counting:** the Section 122 tariff expiry on 24 July 2026 is a macro binary, not a company event, and it cuts both ways. And there is no rate-cut leg in this thesis anywhere — which, with the Fed hawkish and futures pricing meaningful odds of a hike by December, is the right way to be built.

The conclusion the evidence forces: the value here is real but it must be harvested by the buyback grinding the share count down over years, not released by an event over months. Underwrite it on that basis or not at all.
valley_of_death:
The risky window is short, specific and dated: the next two weeks.

The second-quarter report lands on 30 July 2026 against a $0.82 consensus, and management has already told the street this is the soft quarter. On 7 May 2026 they guided core sales down about 1%, with Mobility Technologies down low-to-mid single digits against the $25M Vehicle Identification Solution shipment comparison from the prior year, Environmental and Fueling up only low single digits, and Repair Solutions up low-to-mid single digits. That is a guided-down quarter arriving at a stock that is 12% up its 52-week range, 18% below its 200-day average, and $3.35 off its 52-week low of $27.25.

What makes it dangerous rather than merely dull is the margin line. The first quarter of 2026 already delivered 'adjusted operating margin declined 70 basis points below our expectations' — the first internal miss in five calls — attributed to unfavourable mix and the timing of research spend. Both of those explanations predict recovery; neither has been demonstrated. And the cost programme that is supposed to carry the year is back-half loaded by management's own phasing: about $1M of the $15M landed in the first quarter, about $3M is expected in the second, and roughly $11M — the large majority — is unproven and sits after June. A second consecutive margin miss on 30 July, into a sell-side community already cutting targets (KeyBanc to $35.00 on 13 July, target velocity −14%), is the flush this thesis should wait for. It is precisely the capitulation event that would let a buyer in below $27.

Six days earlier, on 24 July 2026, the Section 122 tariff hits its statutory wall. Vontier quantified roughly $50M of gross tariff cost in 2025 and mitigated it well — China procurement is now under $50M on a run-rate basis, and gross margin held at 47.2% — so the exposure is manageable either way. But the chief financial officer's own first-quarter 2026 language was 'the tariff remains a very dynamic environment,' and a policy scramble in the week before a guided-down print is noise the stock does not need.

A smaller cost tell worth watching: memory-chip prices. Management disclosed it is redesigning printed circuit boards 'to stay ahead of the supply chain issues on memory chips.' The dollar exposure is 'mid- to high single-digit million dollars' — immaterial — but it is consuming engineering capacity, it is the same memory squeeze that produced a $1.3T semiconductor-complex drawdown in late June 2026, and it is a live input-cost creep against a margin guide that is already behind.

What is not in the window, and I want to be clear about it because it is the good news: there is no cash-burn hump and no maturity wall. Vontier generates over $460M of adjusted free cash flow a year at ~15% of sales, converts at ~95%, and carries $1.70B of net debt at roughly 2.2 times EBITDA against a semi-annual bond interest payment of about $19M. Piotroski is 7 of 9. Altman-Z of 2.8 is the grey zone rather than the safe zone, but nothing in the file suggests distress. The risk here is a de-rating and dead money, not solvency.

The deeper valley is not three-to-nine months out — it is the absence of anything at all after 30 July. The catalyst is spent, the buyback has no clock, and the next scheduled event is another earnings print in late October. The realistic bad outcome is not a crash; it is $28 to $32 for four more quarters while the free-cash-flow yield pays you to be patient.
positioning_washout:
There is no mechanical washout coming, and that is a genuine mark against the entry timing rather than in its favour — the forced selling that would hand you a cheap price is not queued up.

The usual mechanism does not apply. Vontier pays only a nominal quarterly dividend (reaffirmed alongside the buyback increase on 19 May 2026), yielding a fraction of a percent. There is no yield-focused shareholder base to expel, no dividend cut to force income funds out, and no pivot that would breach a mandate. Nobody holds this for the income, so nobody is compelled to sell it.

The real dynamic is a slow, discretionary drift rather than a flush, and it has been under way for months. Vontier is a $4.31B market-value, spin-legacy mid-cap in a tape where the money rotated from mega-cap technology into equal-weight indices, and this is a name that does not qualify for either story. It is neither a growth compounder nor a deep-value carcass, so it sits in the gap that gets sold slowly: Eldred Rock Partners cut 51,679 shares on 3 April 2026 from what had been a 4.1% position; twelve months of sell-side targets have drifted from $44.33 to a $39.00 recent average; insiders have made zero open-market purchases against three sales of 24,097 shares. Smart-money score is 31 of 100 and institutional flow is neutral at 50 of 100 — this is a name being quietly de-weighted by discretionary holders, not dumped by a mechanical one.

moderator_conclusion:
My call is to wait for the wash-out — specifically, the second-quarter earnings report on 30 July 2026 — and to size this as a value position with a slow fuse rather than an event.

Here is what Vontier is, stripped of five calls' worth of 'above-market growth' language. It is a flat-revenue, high-margin, cash-generative installed-base annuity that converts about 15% of sales into free cash and returns it through buybacks. Revenue was $2.99B in 2021 and $3.08B in 2025 — a −1.2% three-year compound rate. Earnings per share grow 8-11% a year from margin expansion and a shrinking share count, not from volume. That is a perfectly good thing to own at the right price, and at $30.60 — 8.7 times management's implied 2026 adjusted earnings of about $3.50, an 11% free-cash-flow yield, roughly a third of the way to my $41 sum-of-the-parts base case — the price is right.

The quality is better than the multiple admits, and for reasons that are specific and checkable rather than atmospheric. The payments attach is contractual: 'there is no option in the U.S. to buy a dispenser without our payments' (Q4 2025), and every dispenser Vontier ships in its majority-share home market drags an Invenco kit with it — a nearly $650M business growing 22% organically with 35% recurring revenue. The compliance revenue is regulated: 350,000 automated tank gauges, CARB certification, a replacement cycle in its early innings with 'five plus years' to run. The demand driver is convenience-store capital spending, not fuel volume, and it is accelerating. Management has kept hard promises before — roughly $50M of tariff cost was quantified in the first quarter of 2025 and mitigated to a stable 47.2% gross margin, and China procurement was cut to under $50M on a run-rate basis. They beat six of seven quarters, told the street about Invenco's order lumpiness before it hurt them, and said 'I do not really know what is going on with the consumer this year' rather than spinning it. That is a credible team running a defended base.

The regime helps in one specific and underappreciated way, and hurts in another. It helps on independence: this is a dispersion tape in which the single shared factor that could swamp a book is an artificial-intelligence capital-spending guide-down at late-July hyperscaler earnings, and Vontier's driver is orthogonal to it. Better still, the second shared factor — oil — runs the *right* way here: management's evidence-backed case, laid out in the first quarter of 2026, is that higher fuel prices fatten convenience-store operator margins and fund the modernisation spending Vontier sells into, and that operators plan capital 'two or three years in advance' regardless of oil volatility. There is no rate-cut leg anywhere in this thesis, which is how a thesis should be built with the Fed hawkish and a December hike more likely than a cut. In a book that needs resolution-driver independence, this name earns its slot.

It hurts on the thing that decides sizing. The current tilt rewards structural special situations — spin-offs, forced sellers, distressed — and Vontier is none of them. It was a spin, but six years ago, and the orphan window closed long before I got here. And the catalyst has already fired: the Teletrac Navman sale, the one hard dated event in the file, completed on 6 July 2026 and the stock is still pinned near its 52-week low of $27.25. When management executes its catalyst on schedule and the stock does not move, the market has told you it was not the catalyst. What remains is a $1.0B buyback authorization — roughly 23% of the market value, genuinely powerful arithmetic — attached to no clock whatsoever. And the activists who ought to be circling a name with a visible sum-of-the-parts discount and a chief executive publicly complaining about his own multiple have not shown up, in a year running 136 campaigns with 'sell yourself' the top demand. Their absence is evidence, and the Teletrac terms explain it: $220M of headline value but only $80M in cash, the rest in a seller's note and retained equity, struck in the hottest merger market on record. The private market does not pay peer multiples for these parts either.

So I split the two scores deliberately, because the two questions have genuinely different answers. On value alone — ignoring the catalyst and the tilt entirely — this is a 4: a narrow but real and stable moat, 47.2% gross margins that are not moving, free cash flow compounding at 19% a year, six of seven quarters delivered, and a price a third below a conservatively-trimmed sum-of-the-parts. Note that my $41 base does not require the peer gap to close; it requires it to narrow from roughly half the peer multiple to roughly two-thirds — the discount going from unjustified to merely justified. On the whole package, with the catalyst spent and the tilt pointing elsewhere, it is a 3.

The timing call is the 30 July print, and I want to be precise about why. Management guided that quarter down on 7 May: core sales about −1%, Mobility Technologies down low-to-mid single digits against the $25M Vehicle Identification Solution comparison. The first quarter already delivered the first internal miss in the file — margin 70 basis points 'below our expectations' — and roughly $11M of the $15M savings programme is unproven and sits in the back half. A second consecutive margin miss, into a sell side already backing away (KeyBanc cut to $35.00 on 13 July with the stock at $29.42; target velocity −14%), breaks $27.25 and hands a patient buyer the position at a genuine discount. Insiders, notably, are not competing for it: zero open-market buys against three sales.

I will name the risk in waiting, because it is real and it is the honest argument against my own call. There is no forced seller queued up here — no dividend to cut, no mandate to breach, no mechanical flow. The only thing likely to produce a flush is a bad print. If 30 July is fine and the margin recovers as management claims, the discount starts closing without me and the buyback grinds the share count down while I watch. That is the cost of patience, and I accept it, because the alternative is paying up for a spent catalyst three days before a quarter management has already told me will be soft.

One last thing for the director, on the question that actually decides whether this is cheap or a trap. The obvious fear is the energy transition, and it is why the multiple is 8.7 rather than 15. I judge that threat manageable rather than terminal, and the reasoning matters more than the label: the asset is the store, not the pump — 7-Eleven is remodelling 7,000 sites through 2030 for reasons unrelated to what fills the tank; the payment terminal, the site software and the car-wash brain get paid regardless of energy type; Driivz is the number-two charging-management platform globally at ~110,000 plugs and won Iberdrola/bp pulse's 2,500 fast chargers on 1 July 2026; and underground tanks must be monitored while they exist, which will be decades. The honest bear case here is not 'this melts.' It is 'this never grows, and you are paid 10% a year in cash to wait for a re-rating nobody can force.' That is a price objection, not a quality objection — which is why the value score is a 4 and the moat cap does not bite. But it is also exactly why this is a 3 on the whole and a wait-for-the-flush rather than a buy-now: a company whose value must be harvested by buyback arithmetic over years, rather than released by an event over months, should be bought on a bad day, and 30 July is the most likely bad day on the calendar.

The parts, valued on enterprise-value-to-EBITDA and then netted for debt. peer_comps_note:
The peer file supplies no live override multiples and no anchor multiple, so I built the sum-of-the-parts from segment multiples of my own and used the peer set only as a sanity-check rather than as the anchor — the right order of operations given that peer multiples de-rate and a stale anchor would inflate the apparent discount.

The peer verdict is 'cheap versus peers,' and the direction holds: Vontier's 9.9 times price-to-free-cash-flow is roughly half the ~18-22 times of Dover, Fortive and ITT, and a third of IDEX and Roper at ~28-30 times, against a respectable 47.2% gross margin and 12.8% return on invested capital. But the peer file's own caveat is the honest part and I want to sharpen it. Two-thirds of the gap is earned, not mispriced, and a director should not treat the full spread as alpha:

First, growth. Dover, Fortive, IDEX and Roper are compounders. Vontier's revenue is $3.08B against $2.99B four years ago — a −1.2% three-year compound rate. Half of a compounder's multiple is arithmetically defensible for a company that does not compound revenue.

Second, quality of returns. Roper earns 25%-plus on invested capital; Vontier earns 12.8%. The 51.4% return on equity is a buyback artifact from a shrunk equity base, not an earnings-power signal, and comparing it to peer returns on equity would be an error.

Third, mix. Roughly a fifth of Vontier is Matco Tools, a franchised hand-tool distributor with a wage-pressured customer — a business none of these peers owns and none of these multiples contemplate.

Fourth, leverage. Net debt of $1.70B is roughly 2.2 times EBITDA, heavier than the peer set.

This is not the shared-factor problem — Vontier's discount is idiosyncratic, not sector beta. Dover, Fortive, IDEX and ITT are not de-rated; they trade at full multiples today. The gap is single-name, which means it is genuinely available if it closes. My base case does not require it to close: at $41 Vontier would trade at ~8.9 times free cash flow against the peer set's 18-22 times, moving from roughly half the peer multiple to roughly two-thirds. That is the discount narrowing from unjustified to merely justified — a much lower bar than convergence, and the reason I am comfortable at a $41 base rather than the $43.5 the raw parts produce.

One live market test deserves more weight than any peer multiple: Teletrac Navman, a fixed and cash-generative asset, sold on 6 July 2026 for $220M of headline value but only $80M of cash, with $140M in a seller's note and retained equity. In the hottest merger market on record, that is the only recent independent appraisal of a Vontier asset, and it argues the private market does not pay peer multiples for these parts either.

bull_thesis:
The bull case is that the market is pricing Vontier as a melting fuel-pump maker when what it actually owns is a regulated, contractually-attached convenience-store infrastructure annuity that throws off cash and is buying back its own stock at a tenth of earnings.

Start with the price. At $30.60 a share on the New York Stock Exchange (16 July 2026 close), Vontier's roughly 141 million shares are worth about $4.31B. Management guided to double-digit adjusted earnings growth in 2026 off the $3.20 a share it delivered in 2025 (the four quarters printed $0.77, $0.79, $0.78 and $0.86) — call it about $3.50. That is 8.7 times forward earnings. On cash it is starker: adjusted free cash flow (the cash left after running and investing in the business) was over $460M in 2025, about 15% of sales, and grew 27.9% year over year with a three-year compound rate of 19.1%. Against a $4.31B market value that is a free-cash-flow yield near 11%. Diversified industrial-technology peers — Dover, Fortive (Vontier's former parent), ITT — trade around 18-22 times free cash flow; IDEX and Roper are 28-30 times and up.

Why the base is not melting. Three pieces of evidence from the calls, in ascending order of importance:

First, the demand driver is store capital spending, not fuel volume. Convenience retail is about two-thirds of sales and is growing at a mid-single-digit rate on food service and technology. 7-Eleven has publicly committed to remodel 7,000 North American stores through 2030 plus 1,300 new sites (cited by management, Q1 2026). That capital budget does not care what fills the tank. Management put dated numbers behind the resilience claim on the first-quarter 2026 call: this end market has been durable through 25 years of volatility, and high oil prices have historically been a net positive because fatter fuel margins fund store investment. Environmental and Fueling Solutions has grown at roughly a 6% organic compound rate over the last two years and delivered low-double-digit dispenser growth globally in the first quarter of 2026 with segment margin flat at nearly 30%.

Second, the compliance revenue is regulated. Veeder-Root's automated tank gauges are the instrument that monitors underground fuel storage, with an installed base of over 350,000 units globally, a CARB certification requirement, and a replacement cycle management describes as early innings and 'a pretty steady replacement cycle over the next five plus years' (Q3 2025). One of the largest North American convenience operators signed up to upgrade its entire base across 4,500 sites over five years (Q2 2025). Underground tanks must be monitored while they exist, and they will exist for decades.

Third — and this is the load-bearing fact of the whole thesis — the payments attach is contractual. Asked directly in the fourth quarter of 2025 whether the terminals were a low-margin giveaway used to buy recurring revenue, the chief financial officer answered: 'we sell dispensers with payments. There is no option in the U.S. to buy a dispenser without our payments.' Every dispenser Vontier ships in its majority-share home market pulls an Invenco payment kit with it. Invenco closed 2025 at nearly $650M of revenue, up 22% organically, with recurring revenue at about 35% of its base growing 17%, having passed a billion transactions on its payment servers. Over 50% of new dispensers now leave the factory with a FlexPay 6 unit. The customer's own switching cost is the payment certification bill — 'hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars annually' — which Vontier's single-architecture platform collapses. That is a genuine switching-cost moat, and it is getting deeper as the platform extends to in-store terminals (launched Q4 2025), car washes and chargers.

Why earnings grow even if revenue does not. Vontier's algorithm is margin plus share count, and both are live. Management committed to 80 basis points of operating margin expansion at the midpoint in 2026 and $15M of in-year savings, phased publicly ($1M in Q1, about $3M in Q2, the balance in the back half). It has kept this kind of promise before: roughly $50M of tariff cost was quantified in the first quarter of 2025, mitigated through supply-chain moves and price, and the gross margin held at 47.2% while China procurement was cut to under $50M on a run-rate basis. On capital, the board raised the repurchase authorization to $1.0B on 19 May 2026 — about 23% of the entire market value — and this management actually spends it (roughly $175M through the third quarter of 2025). Book value per share has compounded at 26% over five years. At $30 a share, every dollar of that authorization retires more stock than it did at $45.

The portfolio is being cleaned. The European service business, two non-core assets and a minority equity stake went in 2025; Teletrac Navman — announced 7 May 2026 at a $220M valuation — completed on 6 July 2026, bringing $80M of cash, a $100M seller's note and a retained ~30% stake. Management said the cash goes to 'additional share repurchases and selective bolt-on acquisitions.'

The electric-vehicle question is hedged, not ignored. Driivz manages roughly 110,000 charging plugs and is the number-two platform globally, winning dated business through 2026 (Iberdrola/bp pulse's 2,500 fast chargers on 1 July 2026; Duracell E-Charge's UK network on 11 May 2026). If the forecourt electrifies, Vontier still sells the payment terminal, the site software and the car wash brain.

Conditions that must hold: convenience-retail capital spending stays constructive through 2027; the back-half-weighted $15M savings actually lands and the first-quarter margin miss proves to be mix and research-spend timing as claimed; Invenco's order lumpiness does not turn into order loss; and the board keeps buying stock aggressively at these levels rather than spending the authorization on acquisitions.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is simple and it has been right for four years: Vontier does not grow, cannot force anyone to notice, and the discount is not a mistake — it is the market's price for a flat business with a finite runway and no clock on it.

Start with the number management does not lead with. Revenue was $2.99B in 2021 and $3.08B in 2025. That is +0.7% in total across four years — a three-year revenue compound rate of −1.2%. Reported earnings per share went from $2.43 in 2021 to $2.76 in 2025, a 3.5% compound rate. The 11% adjusted growth management celebrates is margin and buyback arithmetic performed on a stationary base. Buy this and you are underwriting a financial engine, not a business engine — and financial engines re-rate only when someone forces them to.

Nobody is going to force it. This is the heart of the bear case. The one hard, dated corporate event in the file has already happened: the Teletrac divestiture closed on 6 July 2026, and the stock is $30.60 — near its 52-week low of $27.25, 18% below its 200-day average, and sitting 12% up its 52-week range. Management has been telling anyone who will listen that the stock is too cheap — 'our shares remain meaningfully discounted to peers, underscoring the upside as we continue to execute' (Q3 2025 closing remarks) — which is exactly what a management team says when it has run out of levers. And the people who would know are not buying. Zero open-market insider purchases against three sales totalling 24,097 shares. The chief executive calls his own stock meaningfully discounted and buys none of it.

The Teletrac terms tell you what the assets are actually worth. In the hottest merger market on record — roughly $2.8T announced in the first half of 2026 — a business management describes as a completed multi-year turnaround with reduced churn, mid-single-digit recurring-revenue growth and positive free cash flow fetched $220M of headline value but only $80M of cash. The operating story is already cracking. Management told the street on 7 May 2026 to expect core sales down about 1% in the second quarter, with Mobility Technologies down low-to-mid single digits against a $25M Vehicle Identification Solution shipment comparison, and about $11M of the $15M savings programme still unproven in the back half. Target velocity is −14%. The sell side is walking its numbers down toward the price, not up toward the thesis.

A fifth of the company is genuinely impaired. Matco Tools sells hand tools off franchisee trucks to wage-pressured auto technicians. Sell-out was down about 5% in the first half of 2025; management called the consumer 'a harder time with their pocketbook' and admitted in the fourth quarter of 2025, 'I do not really know what is going on with the consumer this year.' The terminal question is real, and being cheap does not answer it. The installed base is fuel dispensers and underground petroleum tanks. Over a fifteen-to-twenty-year horizon, electrification shrinks the fuelling stops, the fuel volume and eventually the tank count. The hedge — Driivz — is unquantified: management gave it a full, enthusiastic answer in the first quarter of 2025 ('#2 worldwide... it is a SaaS business at very high margins... it will actually begin to show up at the Vontier level') and has not put a revenue number on it in a single call since, while continuing to issue press releases about it. The balance sheet removes the margin for error. moderator_conclusion:
My call is to wait for the wash-out — specifically, the second-quarter earnings report on 30 July 2026 — and to size this as a value position with a slow fuse rather than an event.

Here is what Vontier is, stripped of five calls' worth of 'above-market growth' language. Revenue was $2.99B in 2021 and $3.08B in 2025 — a −1.2% three-year compound rate. Earnings per share grow 8-11% a year from margin expansion and a shrinking share count, not from volume. The regime helps in one specific and underappreciated way, and hurts in another. Better still, the second shared factor — oil — runs the *right* way here: management's evidence-backed case, laid out in the first quarter of 2026, is that higher fuel prices fatten convenience-store operator margins and fund the modernisation spending Vontier sells into, and that operators plan capital 'two or three years in advance' regardless of oil volatility. It hurts on the thing that decides sizing. The current tilt rewards structural special situations — spin-offs, forced sellers, distressed — and Vontier is none of them. It was a spin, but six years ago, and the orphan window closed long before I got here. And the catalyst has already fired: the Teletrac Navman sale, the one hard dated event in the file, completed on 6 July 2026 and the stock is still pinned near its 52-week low of $27.25. The first quarter already delivered the first internal miss in the file — margin 70 basis points 'below our expectations' — and roughly $11M of the $15M savings programme is unproven and sits in the back half. I will name the risk in waiting, because it is real and it is the honest argument against my own call. peer_comps_note:
The peer file supplies no live override multiples and no anchor multiple, so I built the sum-of-the-parts from segment multiples of my own and used the peer set only as a sanity-check rather than as the anchor — the right order of operations given that peer multiples de-rate and a stale anchor would inflate the apparent discount.

The peer verdict is 'cheap versus peers,' and the direction holds: Vontier's 9.9 times price-to-free-cash-flow is roughly half the ~18-22 times of Dover, Fortive and ITT, and a third of IDEX and Roper at ~28-30 times, against a respectable 47.2% gross margin and 12.8% return on invested capital. First, growth. Dover, Fortive, IDEX and Roper are compounders. Vontier's revenue is $3.08B against $2.99B four years ago — a −1.2% three-year compound rate. Half of a compounder's multiple is arithmetically defensible for a company that does not compound revenue.

Second, quality of returns. Roper earns 25%-plus on invested capital; Vontier earns 12.8%. The 51.4% return on equity is a buyback artifact from a shrunk equity base, not an earnings-power signal, and comparing it to peer returns on equity would be an error.

Third, mix. Roughly a fifth of Vontier is Matco Tools, a franchised hand-tool distributor with a wage-pressured customer — a business none of these peers owns and none of these multiples contemplate.

Fourth, leverage. Net debt of $1.70B is roughly 2.2 times EBITDA, heavier than the peer set.

This is not the shared-factor problem — Vontier's discount is idiosyncratic, not sector beta. Dover, Fortive, IDEX and ITT are not de-rated; they trade at full multiples today. The gap is single-name, which means it is genuinely available if it closes. My base case does not require it to close: at $41 Vontier would trade at ~8.9 times free cash flow against the peer set's 18-22 times, moving from roughly half the peer multiple to roughly two-thirds.
